terms.definition: Address Resolution Protocol — how devices on a local network translate an IP address into the hardware (MAC) address needed to actually deliver a packet.
Bridge Protocol Data Unit — control frames sent between network switches to run the Spanning Tree Protocol and elect a root bridge.
Basic Service Set Identifier — the unique MAC address that identifies a specific wireless access point radio, distinct from the SSID network name.
When a network loop causes the same frame to be forwarded repeatedly and infinitely, flooding bandwidth and making the network unusable within seconds.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System — a 0–10 scale that rates how severe a software vulnerability is; 9+ is Critical, 7–8.9 is High, 4–6.9 is Medium.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — the service that automatically assigns IP addresses to devices when they join a network so you do not have to configure each one manually.
Domain Name System — translates human-readable names like 'google.com' into the IP addresses that computers actually use to route traffic.
When DNS queries are sent to your ISP's servers instead of a private resolver (e.g. a VPN's DNS), revealing your browsing activity to your ISP.
Discover-Offer-Request-Acknowledge — the four-message sequence a device uses to request and receive an IP address from a DHCP server.
The router or device that connects your local network to the internet; all traffic destined for external IP addresses is sent here first.
The variation in latency between successive packets — high jitter causes choppy audio/video calls even when average latency looks fine.
The time it takes for a packet to travel from your device to a destination and back (round-trip time), measured in milliseconds.
Media Access Control address — a unique 12-character hardware identifier burned into every network interface; the first 6 characters (OUI) identify the manufacturer.
Multicast DNS — a zero-configuration protocol that lets devices find each other by name (e.g. 'printer.local') on a local network without a central DNS server.
My TraceRoute — a network diagnostic tool that combines ping and traceroute to show every router hop between you and a destination, with latency at each hop.
Organizationally Unique Identifier — the first 3 bytes of a MAC address assigned to a specific hardware manufacturer; used to identify what type of device is on your network.
The percentage of packets sent that never arrive at the destination; anything above 1% causes noticeable degradation in real-time applications like video calls.
Quality of Service — router settings that prioritise certain types of traffic (e.g. video calls over file downloads) to maintain performance during congestion.
The standard that defines the three private IP address ranges (10.x.x.x, 172.16–31.x.x, 192.168.x.x) used inside home and office networks, not routable on the internet.
An unknown device on your network — could be an intruder, a misconfigured IoT device, or a guest device that was never removed.
Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio — a measure of 5G/LTE signal quality; above 20 dB is excellent, below 0 dB means interference dominates the signal.
Simple Network Management Protocol — used by routers, switches, and servers to report status metrics and receive management commands from monitoring tools.
Service Set Identifier — the name of a Wi-Fi network as broadcast by an access point; multiple access points can share the same SSID to form one seamless network.
Spanning Tree Protocol — automatically detects and blocks network loops by disabling redundant switch ports, preventing broadcast storms.
A logical subdivision of a network; devices on the same /24 subnet share the first three octets of their IP address (e.g. 192.168.1.x) and can communicate directly.
The three-message sequence (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK) that establishes a reliable connection between two devices before any data is exchanged.
Transport Layer Security — the encryption protocol behind HTTPS; it authenticates the server and encrypts data in transit to prevent eavesdropping.
A diagnostic tool that reveals every router hop between your device and a destination, with the latency at each hop — useful for pinpointing where delays occur.
The percentage of time a device or service was reachable over a given period; 99.9% uptime still means about 8.7 hours of downtime per year.
Virtual Local Area Network — a logical network partition that isolates groups of devices (e.g. IoT devices from work laptops) even when they share the same physical switches.
